title: Beautiful Studio Ghibli coin/card cases recreate scenes and props from anime classics [Photos]
description: What better place to carry your train pass than inside No Face’s Spirited Away train ride? In Japan, the vast majority of transactions involve either coins or a card. Yen coins go all the way up to 500 yen (US$3.15) in denomination, so it’s inevitable that you’re going to accumulate a handful of change if […]
content:
What better place to carry your train pass than inside No Face’s Spirited Away train ride?

In Japan, the vast majority of transactions involve either coins or a card. Yen coins go all the way up to 500 yen (US$3.15) in denomination, so it’s inevitable that you’re going to accumulate a handful of change if you’re using cash to buy things or pay for meals, and rechargeable train pass cards like Suica can also be used for purchases at shops and restaurants.

So if you’re traveling in Japan, a card or coin case is a handy thing to have, and a Ghibli anime case is a handy thing to have that’s also awesome.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has designed a series of combination coin/card cases featuring artifacts and characters from some of their most beloved animated films. Starting things off is this embroidered trio of No Face, Boh, and Yu-Bird taking a ride on the train seen in Spirited Away.

The reverse side of the case features the film’s name and an understated illustration, and when you open up the zipper, and you’ll find two compartments inside, allowing a layer of organization for different types of coins or cards.

Other charming details include Boh and Yu-Bird taking a nap on the extendable strap’s connecting-piece reel and a caterpillar-shaped zipper pull.

An especially clever design point is that the windows on the train are actually see-through, adding to the illusion that the characters are actually passing by scenery outside their train carriage.

▼ Though Boh and Yu-Bird are kind of in the emperor of Japan’s seat.

Next up we have another Ghibli character depicted in his most memorable setting: Calcifer peeking out from a cast-iron frying pan.

The Howl’s Moving Castle fire spirit is in the middle of cooking up the hearty breakfast seen in the movie, one of the most mouthwatering of all Ghibli meals. Fittingly, the zipper pull for this pouch is shaped like a spoon, while the strap-connecting piece is a recreation of the multicolored dial next to the castle’s front door that allows the dwelling’s entrance to magically connect to different locations.

The Calcifer pouch is the only one we’re looking at today with only a single shared interior section, so we’re back to two compartments for the My Neighbor Totoro case.

Instead of being shaped like the cuddly studio mascot himself, this pouch is modeled after the container of caramels that sisters Mei and Satsuki share some snacks from early in the movie while they ride in the back of the moving truck on their way to their new home in the most idyllic of Ghibli countrysides.

You do get some Totoro embroidery on the front of the pouch, though, and hanging out around back, as well as on the strap connector, are a bunch of Soot Sprites…

…and the zipper pull this time is caramel-shaped.

And finally, while it may not be candy-related, the fourth pouch is also very sweet…

…since it’s modeled on the party invitation that Tombo gives to enterprising witch Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service.

As is often the case with Kiki’s merchandise, black cat Jiji is more prominently featured that the titular protagonist herself, though Kiki’s likeness, of a sort, does still appear on the reel and zipper pull.

Though there’s a lot of variety in the designs, they’re all identically priced at 3,190 yen (US$20). Though the Whisper of the Heart book-design pouch seen at the very start of this article is still out of stock, all of the others have recently been restocked and are available through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.

Source: Donguri Kyowakoku

title: Japan restarts at-home collection agent visits for public TV fees
description: Japan’s public broadcaster will once again send third-party agents to people’s doors, resuming unpopular tactic of collecting quasi-obligated fees. Imagine you’re sitting at home, and all of a sudden there’s a knock at the door. You go to see who it is, and it turns out to be someone saying that you have to give […]
content:
Japan’s public broadcaster will once again send third-party agents to people’s doors, resuming unpopular tactic of collecting quasi-obligated fees.

Imagine you’re sitting at home, and all of a sudden there’s a knock at the door. You go to see who it is, and it turns out to be someone saying that you have to give them some money, right then and there, to fulfil your civic duty of funding the police or fire department.

That’d be pretty strange. Generally, things that are supposed to be public services are supposed to be funded through tax revenues, not by individual organizations showing up at your home with an outstretched palm. And it would be even weirder if the person asking you for money was not themselves part of the police or fire department, right? And yet, for many years, this was how Japan’s public broadcaster, NHK, did things. NHK would contract with third-party, private-company bill collectors, who would show up at people’s homes, including at night, and ask for money if they didn’t have a record of the occupant having paid their NHK fees recently.

This, as you might imagine, was not a visit that any members of the public enjoyed getting, especially given the aggressive tone and shady tactics some collection agents employed. After years of blowback, in 2023 NHK finally did away with the practice of at-home visits by third-party collection agents, but on Monday, they announced that they’re bringing them back.

NHK fees exist in an unusual legal space. According to Japan’s Broadcasting Act, anyone with a device that is able to receive NHK broadcasts is required to pay an annual fee of 12,276 yen (US$77), and for those with devices capable of receiving not just NHK’s terrestrial broadcasts but their satellite one as well, the free rises to 21,765 yen a year (those who don’t want to cough up a whole year’s worth of fees all at once can opt for a two or six-month plan, but at higher per-month rates).

Note that actually watching the broadcast is not stipulated as being part of the condition for payment. Simply having a TV that receives NHK broadcasts, which TVs sold in Japan do by default, is enough, and NHK holds that since they produce online content as well, now any household where at least one person has a smartphone, tablet, or Internet-connected PC has to pay too.

▼ So score one for anyone who’s still holding out with an old-school cell phone.

Here, though, is where things get messy. That same Broadcast Act that says people have to pay NHK fees? It doesn’t include any sort of punishment for non-compliance. The fact that NHK apparently can’t just receive an equivalent cut from tax revenue, nor is able to send out payment notices that recipients legally have to comply with, casts further doubt on just how legit the system really is. The use of third-party collectors, and also some embezzlement/accounting scandals within NHK, haven’t helped the public broadcaster’s image either, nor inspired confidence that they’re appropriately using the money they do collect.

But NHK is unhappy with the amount of fees it’s been collecting recently, saying that the 585.1 billion yen it gathered in 2025 was down 5 billion yen from the year before. The organization is also concerned that this was the seventh year in a row for fee collection revenue to decline.

▼ Japan’s total population has also been declining for seven years in a row (more than seven, actually), but I’m sure that demographic detail just slipped NHK’s mind.

So NHK will once again be having third-party agents to go to people’s homes and ask them to pay up if they haven’t already. The program has already resumed in parts of Osaka and Hyogo Prefectures, and the current plan is to expand it to large cities like Tokyo and Nagoya first, followed by a potential further spread to smaller-sized communities.

If you’re wondering whether NHK has to pay the collection agents, the answer is yes, and agents get paid higher amounts the more fees they collect. As a matter of fact, NHK has had to reduce the amount they’ll be paying collection agents compared to previous rates, as costs associated with the old arrangement were deemed too high.

NHK is, at least, aware of the bad reputation these tactics have earned them in the past, and is trying to do things a little less abrasively this time around. Instead of sudden, unannounced visits, written notices will be mailed to households first, with in-person visits coming later. It’s not clear whether those who receive a notice will be asked to schedule a visit, or if it’s just a unilateral declaration of when the agent will be coming. The goal, though, is to “achieve understanding and receive payment of fees through polite explanation,” so hopefully no one else is going to get their house tagged for nonpayment.

Source: Sankei Shimbun via Jin, Yomiuri Shimbun, Asahi Shimbun, Japan Times, Bloomberg

title: Converse Japan and one of Japan’s greatest painters combine for fine fowl shoes [Photos]
description: An all-star of the Edo period art world graces a new canvas. The defining detail of Converse’s All Stars series of sneakers is that the shoes are made with canvas. Of course, linguistically, “canvas” can refer not only to sturdy woven fabric, but also a space in which an artist can create, and both of […]
content:
An all-star of the Edo period art world graces a new canvas.

The defining detail of Converse’s All Stars series of sneakers is that the shoes are made with canvas. Of course, linguistically, “canvas” can refer not only to sturdy woven fabric, but also a space in which an artist can create, and both of those meanings apply to Converse Japan’s newest model.

These hi-top kicks are called the All Star IJ HI, and while scholars of classical Japanese painting may be saying “Ah, of course!” as they look at the IJ part of the name, we’ll take a moment to delve into the letters’ significance. Actually, the IJ here is a set of initials, referring to Ito Jakuchu, one of the most celebrated artists of the mid-Edo period.

▼ Ito Jakuchu

Born in 1712, Ito started out life as a grocer who took over his father’s business in Kyoto’s Nishiki Market (the same market that’s now become a major tourist attraction). But what Ito really wanted to do was paint, and what he really wanted to paint was birds…and the birds he really, really wanted to paint were chickens and roosters.

Though they weren’t his only subject matter, Ito found fowl such fine muses that he painted multiple pieces with gunkeizu, or “painting of chickens/roosters” in their title. For the All Star IJ HI, Converse Japan has chosen to adorn the shoes’ canvas with imagery from Ito’s Saboten Gunkeizu, which Ito painted on the sliding doors of Osaka’s Saifukuji Temple in 1789.

▼ Incidentally, while Converse was founded in the U.S. and has been a subsidiary of Nike since 2003, Converse Japan is a separate company, and part of Japan’s Itochu trading company conglomerate.

Having lived his entire life in the Edo period, when Japan was closed off to the rest of the world by decree of the Tokugawa Shogunate, Ito himself would have had little, if any, opportunity to see footwear beyond traditional geta and zori sandals. Nevertheless, his painting makes for a very stylish sneaker motif, mixing bold and colorful imagery without crossing the line into being garish.

The All Star JB HI is priced at 14,300 yen (US$90) and availably exclusively through Japanese shore store ABC Mart, with orders placeable through the chain’s online store here.

title: Bear found on Japanese fishing boat, escapes into the sea
description: Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the water… Long-time readers of news in Japan will undoubtedly know that we have something of a bear problem. Dwindling human populations in rural areas abandoning farms and homes have allowed a growing ursine population an opportunity to roam further in search of food. […]
content:
Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the water…

Long-time readers of news in Japan will undoubtedly know that we have something of a bear problem. Dwindling human populations in rural areas abandoning farms and homes have allowed a growing ursine population an opportunity to roam further in search of food. As a result, people and bears are increasingly coming face to face, often with tragic results.

And yet, with the vast majority of Japan’s population residing in urban areas, most of us feel like it’s not our problem. Even as bold as they’ve been becoming, bears still tend to stick to the mountains, so as long as we stay away from those, we stay away from bears.

It’s a luxury that fishermen also once enjoyed. After all, it’s not like a bear’s going to suddenly appear out on the open sea… right?

Such a scene was only narrowly avoided when a bear was found hiding out on a fishing boat docked on the coast of Shiogama, Miyagi Prefecture. On 19 September, the one-meter-tall bear was initially spotted on the wharf but took shelter in a longline tuna fishing boat nearby when police arrived.

▼ News report on the potential stowaway bear

The boat had three crew members on board who hid inside private cabins while the animal was roaming the decks. Meanwhile, police cordoned off the area and city officials also arrived to help monitor the bear’s movements.

They planned to wait until dawn to order local hunters in to kill the bear, but at around 1 a.m. the bear evaded local law enforcement by jumping from the boat and into the sea. Authorities monitored the nearby shoreline to see where it would surface but were unable to find the animal.

Bears have shown a very strong talent for evading police cordons in the past as well. That, combined with the fact that it only appeared to be innocently roaming around without injuring anyone, made it hard to not feel a little good that the situation was resolved without any human or animal getting hurt. As such, many online comments were quick with jokes about it.

“Looks like it ‘bearly’ got away!”
“Bear has learned the unique skill: Bear Swim.”
“A bear that doesn’t swim is just an ordinary bear.”
“Imagine going to the beach and seeing a bear swim in from the sea.”
“It’s surprising how many people know bears can swim really well.”
“Maybe it just wanted to apply for a job.”
“Shark bear.”
“If that bear managed to sneak aboard while they set sail, it would have been a perfect b-movie plot.”
“Bears are everywhere!”

That last comment is probably the key takeaway from all this. With each passing year, there are fewer and fewer places in Japan where we can safely say, “Well, at least I don’t have to worry about getting attacked by a bear here.”

But it still seems as if very little is being done to address the issue. Japan’s hunters are getting older with each passing year, and few younger people are interested enough to overcome the country’s strict gun laws to take up such work. Hopefully, those in the national government nestled in a relatively bear-free part of Metropolitan Tokyo won’t choose to ignore this particular problem until it swims up and bites them in the ass.

Source: TBS News Dig, Hachima Kiko

title: New Cardcaptor Sakura fashion line delivers magical girl style for real-world ladies
description: Anime-inspired looks with for-fans nods to the classic series. Creative costumes are a hallmark of the magical girl anime genre, and while Japanese fashion brand Axes Femme may not be able to provide you with a sparkly transformation sequence, they are ready to give fans a new line of Cardcaptor Sakura apparel items. These aren’t […]
content:
Anime-inspired looks with for-fans nods to the classic series.

Creative costumes are a hallmark of the magical girl anime genre, and while Japanese fashion brand Axes Femme may not be able to provide you with a sparkly transformation sequence, they are ready to give fans a new line of Cardcaptor Sakura apparel items.

These aren’t full-blown cosplay items that recreate Sakura’s in-anime outfits with 1:1 fidelity, though. Instead, they’re playfully stylish creations that incorporate the visual motifs and iconography of the series in ways that can still be used in non-magical settings too, with separate tops and bottoms that allow you to put together an entire outfit or mix an item in with your preexisting non-Cardcaptor wardrobe.

Starting things off is the Cardcaptor Sakura Cardigan, which comes in not just four colors, but four character themes. Pictured above is the pink Sakura Kinomoto version, and while all four designs feature frog-clasp closures and lacy accents on the sleeves, only Sakura’s has an embroidered crest of cherry blossom petals, feathers, and stars surrounded by rhinestones.

Alternatively, the lavender Tomoyo cardigan’s crest has musical notes and sakura petals. A compass is the crest for the minty green Syaoran design, and the snowflakes found on the back of the Clow and Sakura books represent Yue on the white cardigan.

The same character-inspired color schemes are utilized for Axes Femme’s Cardcaptor Sakura berets, although the Syaroan version is a less minty shade of green.

Aside from the different colors, the designs for the berets are identical, with each featuring embroidered wings, a tassel, and a Kero-chan charm.

Options are a little more limited for the skirts, which have a flowing sequence of embroidered Clow, Sakura, and Clear Cards amidst suns, moons, and cherry blossoms.

The two-tone design, though, means that each of the three designs gives you a double-dose of colors to coordinate with.

If it’s not chilly enough to use a cardigan, there are alternate top options with a pair of blouses.

The high collar features an asymmetrical pattern with the sun on one side and the moon on the other. Also, look closely and you’ll see that the lace trim on the cuffs has little Kero-chans in it!

Speaking of collars, you might have noticed that the photo of the pink cardigan up above features one that’s especially elaborate. This is actually a separate item.

Though the floral/feathery flares are always white, the attachable collar comes in two color schemes for the ribbon and embroidered wings and Sakura Card emblem.

Finally, rounding out the collection is a trio of stoles, combining the card motif of the skirts with the lace trim of the blouses/skirt hems.

Prices range from 4,400 yen (US$28) for the beret to 5,500 yen for the collar and stole, 7,700 yen for the blouse and cardigan, and 9,900 yen for the skirt. The entire lineup is available through the Axes Femme online shop here.

title: Famous Kyoto shrine has a message for foreign tourists who think it’s okay to dance at sacred sites
description: Fushimi Inari Taisha asks visitors to show some respect after dance videos filmed beneath its famous torii gates spark criticism online. One of the things that draws tourists to Kyoto is its shrines and temples, which have been beautifully preserved for centuries. However, as the world changes around these historic sites, new problems have cropped […]
content:
Fushimi Inari Taisha asks visitors to show some respect after dance videos filmed beneath its famous torii gates spark criticism online.

One of the things that draws tourists to Kyoto is its shrines and temples, which have been beautifully preserved for centuries. However, as the world changes around these historic sites, new problems have cropped up, including overtourism and the desire for fame and likes on social media.

As a result, one of Kyoto’s most famous shrines, Fushimi Inari Taisha, has recently become the stage for a number of individuals who think it’s okay to perform dances on its sacred grounds, all in a bid to gain views. After these videos were widely circulated online, they received a fair amount of clapback from viewers who criticised the thoughtless acts, and now the shrine itself has come forward with a message in response to the social media storm.

One of the recent videos, shared on TikTok and Twitter in early September, showed foreign tourists dancing beneath the shrine’s famous torii gates, blocking the path of other visitors who could be seen waiting for the group to finish their routine. Not only were they blocking the path, but members of the group could be seen entering from outside the walkway, interfering with the natural environment, which according to Shinto religion, is considered sacred.

In fact, the entire grounds is considered sacred, including the approach, where a group of Maori women from New Zealand recently filmed themselves while performing a traditional poi dance. This clip was also met with criticism from the wider community, including from New Zealand-born professional wrestler Henare, who is of Maori heritage. He pointed out that dancing in sacred places also goes against Maori customs and apologised for the incident. He said he had tracked down the people involved and asked them to make a substantial donation to Fushimi Inari Taisha as an apology.

▼ The approach is said to be the pathway for the gods, and is so sacred that etiquette dictates visitors should walk on the sides rather than the very middle.

With other dance videos being filmed at the site and shared online, Fushimi Inari Taisha responded on 7 September with a notice in both Japanese and English reminding visitors to observe proper manners. It explained that the shrine grounds are a sacred area and place of prayer with more than 1,300 years of history.

In an interview with Japanese media outlet J-Cast News, the shrine confirmed that videos had indeed been filmed on its grounds and went on to say that staff will approach visitors whenever they spot prohibited or disruptive behaviour.

Although no damage had been reported in connection with the dancing, the shrine said it was disappointed that these visitors failed to understand the cultural significance of the site.

It’s worth remembering that although shrines like Fushimi Inari Taisha are places of beauty, they are not dance studios, and they are not spaces owned by tourists. They are places where spirits reside, gods are worshipped, and people come to pray. And as more people become familiar with temple and shrine etiquette in Japan, the video that you think will go viral might just land you in hot water and leave you being cancelled instead.

Sources: J-Cast News via Jin, Yahoo! Japan News

title: Studio Ghibli releases new plush mascot character collection with a focus on friendship
description: Unlikely friendships form across anime movie borders with this new range of soft plush toys. One of the big things that makes a Studio Ghibli film so magical is its characters. A lot of the time, though, the most charming characters tend to be the most elusive, hiding out in forests, bathhouses and even a […]
content:
Unlikely friendships form across anime movie borders with this new range of soft plush toys.


One of the big things that makes a Studio Ghibli film so magical is its characters. A lot of the time, though, the most charming characters tend to be the most elusive, hiding out in forests, bathhouses and even a castle in the sky.

Now there’s a way to befriend these characters in real life, and we don’t have to search high and low for them, as they’re being made available in the form of soft plushies at Ghibli’s specialty retail chain Donguri Kyowakoku.

Called “Nakayoshi Mascot“, this collection of cute characters puts the focus on “nakayoshi”, a concept in Japanese that focuses on harmony and getting along well. Under this banner, the plushies are designed to get along with their human owners and each other as well, so that unlikely friendships can be formed across traditional movie borders.

There are 11 characters vying for our attention in the range, starting with the My Neighbor Totoro Nakayoshi Mascots.

▼ Large Totoro (1,980 yen)

The character that we would usually refer to as “Totoro” is actually known as “Large Totoro” in Japan, to help distinguish it from the smaller ones seen in the movie. Despite the name, it stands at around the same height as the smaller Totoros in this collection, at 9 × 9.5 × 9 centimetres (3.5 × 3.7 × 3.5 inches).

▼ All three Nakayoshi Mascot Totoros look as cute from behind as they do from the front, thanks to their plump little tails.

▼ Large Totoro Leaf (2,090 yen)

Because one Totoro just isn’t enough, the collection includes another Large Totoro, this time with a soft leaf, referencing the large leaf that it holds in the film.

▼ Medium Totoro (1,980 yen)

The Medium Totoro brings its blue hues to the range, and is only a tad smaller, at 10 × 8.5 × 8 centimetres.

▼ Small Totoro (1,650 yen)

The Small Totoro, at 8.5 × 5.5 × 8 centimetres  is smaller again, and is particularly adorable with its large eyes and mouthless features imploring us to take it home.

▼ Catbus (2,420 yen)

The grinning Catbus looks even cuter in soft miniature form, and although it towers over the other characters in the movie, here it measures in at 6 × 8.5 × 12.5 centimetres, making it fit in nicely with the other friends in the collection.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service – Jiji (2,090 yen)

Moving over to the magical world of Kiki’s Delivery Service, we have the beloved feline from the film representing, with limbs wide open as if it’s waiting for a cuddle.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service – Lily (2,090 yen)

Jiji may not have Kiki by his side for this adventure, but girlfriend Lily will gladly keep him company.

▼ Spirited Away – Otori sama (1,980 yen)

The big yellow bath-loving birds from Spirited Away bring their charm to the Nakayoshi range, while Boh Mouse reminds us of the firm friendship that forms between very different characters in the movie.

▼ Spirited Away – Boh Mouse (2,090 yen)

▼ Laputa: Castle in the Sky – Fox Squirrel (2,200 yen)

One of the friendliest furry animals in the world of Ghibli has to be the beautiful fox squirrels from Laputa: Castle in the Sky. Pop this little plushie on your shoulder and you’ll feel like the giant robot, or even Nausicaä from Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, who also befriends these creatures in her universe.

▼ Princess Mononoke – Kodama (1,650 yen)

Some of the most memorable characters in Princess Mononoke are the bobble-headed kodama that clack away in the forest, exuding an otherworldly, mystical charm. This kodama retains the wide-eyed, off-kilter features that help to maintain its mystique, but is wonderfully soft so you can give it all the friendly cuddles it needs.

This is a very sweet collection of friends that we’re more than happy to welcome into our home, and they can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below). It’ll be tough to choose our favourites, but the temptation to purchase from across the Ghibli worlds to create our own crossover storylines is way too great to resist.

Source: Donguri Kyowakoku

Adenot isn’t the only one making her maiden voyage beyond Earth’s gravitation pull, though, as she’s been accompanied […]
content:
Shared spirit of adventure leads to team-up between Pokémon franchise ahead of World Space Week.

French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on her first trip to space, as part of the European Space Agency’s ongoing Epsilon mission. Adenot isn’t the only one making her maiden voyage beyond Earth’s gravitation pull, though, as she’s been accompanied by another first-time spacefarer: a Pikachu.

Adenot blasted off back in February from Cape Canaveral, but as revealed in a just-released video that was recorded prior to her departure, Adenot took a Pikachu plushie, dressed in an ESA uniform, with her to the International Space Station.

The reveal coincides with the announcement that Pokémon Company is helping promote the ESA’s World Space Week events, which will be taking place from October 4 to 10. The ESA says that the two organizations’ shared values of curiosity and imagination and spirit of adventure are the result of “a common ambition: to inspire new generations to dream big, explore and experiment.”

As part of the celebration, there are two new Pikachu plushies on the way, one male and one female (female Pikachus have a heart-shaped tail tip), as well as crossover pins, patches, tote bags, apparel, and Pokémon Trading Card Game accessories coming to both the Pokémon Center and ESA online stores.

▼ There’s no word as to whether Sailor Moon’s Artemis was part of the ground control team for the Pikachu plushie’s spaceflight.

Though Pokémon is best known for its in-game/anime pseudo-science such as Dragon-type attacks being ineffective against Fairy-type Pokémon or Eevee only being able to evolve into Umbreon under the light of the moon, in recent years the franchise has partnered with a number of educational, scientific, and cultural organizations, as seen in the Pokémon Fossil Museum events, the Pokémon x Crafts Exhibition, and Amsterdam Van Gogh Museum collaboration.

Full details regarding prices and on-sale dates for the Pokémon/ESA crossover merch are yet to be released, but ostensibly they should be available by the start of World Space Week on October 4.

Related: Pokémon Center, ESA online shop

title: Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword gets real-world practicality as a giant towel [Photos]
description: The fantasy of using Cloud’s sword every day can now become a reality. Even within that artistic subgenre, though, Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword is an especially extreme example. Right off the bat, […]
content:
The fantasy of using Cloud’s sword every day can now become a reality.

There’s a whole lot of imagery in anime and video games that looks awesome but would be impractical in the real world. Even within that artistic subgenre, though, Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword is an especially extreme example.

Right off the bat, it’s a sword, something that most of us don’t have a use for in our daily lives. Should you somehow happen to have a melee weapon-intensive lifestyle, even then the Buster Sword isn’t a particularly viable choice, since while protagonist Cloud can swing the thing around with ease, it’d be too heavy and bulky to fight with for those of us who have to deal with actual weight and gravity without any assistance from an in-game physics engine.

And yet…the Buster Sword does look really cool, so thankfully Square Enix has come up with a version that can serve a useful purpose for those of us not living in the world of Final Fantasy.

Draped over that dude’s back is the Final Fantasy VII Buster Sword Muffler Towel. Muffler towels (muffler here being used to indicate a scarf, not a part of a car’s exhaust system) are essentially a long face towel, made of material that’s pliable enough to drape over your shoulders or wrap around your neck. A lot of muffler towels bear the names and insignias of sports teams, bands, or idol singers, but this one instead features a print of Cloud’s Buster Sword.

▼ The reverse-side has longer loops to better wick away moisture.

Muffler towels are especially popular at fan events, where dampening them with water before putting one on your shoulders is a great way to counteract the heat generated by large crowds. With a length of 128.5 centimeters (50.6 inches), though, the Buster Sword towel is large enough to make a striking statement as home décor, hung on a wall or next to a sink.

It’s available for preorder through the Square Enix online store here, priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50) and with a release date of December 19. Just make sure your cat doesn’t get it mixed up with its Buster Sword scratching pad.

title: Denny’s Mapputatsu? Parfait is hiding a big secret in plain sight that splits us down the middle
description: The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone. Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to […]
content:
The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone.

Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to its name, the Mapputatsu? Parfait (“Two equal parts? Parfait”).

▼ Pictured below are versions with Shine Muscat grapes for 1,078 yen (US$6.87) and with chocolate for 748 yen.

The purpose of this unusual setup is to reduce food waste while still providing a visually attractive, photo-worthy treat for diners. The menu even provides statistics that 54 percent of diners have ordered food for the sake of posting photos on social media and one out of three have left their dessert unfinished at family-style restaurants in Japan. With parfaits typically looking like veritable works of food art but also being on the larger side, we can assume that they’re one of the more common menu items that diners order for the visual spectacle but aren’t able to finish.

Initially, the Mapputatsu? Parfait was only available at two Denny’s Japan locations, but it’s been slowly expanding onto menus across the country. We happened to be in the area of Saitama-Shintoshin’s Cocoon City shopping complex branch recently and decided to swing by to finally try it out.

Once we sat down and peeked at the digital tablet menu, we were excited to see it in all of its question-asking glory. It was a tough choice but we ordered the Shine Muscat version.

It arrived about 10 minutes later. We took a moment to admire its striking visuals from head-on, the way the waiter had placed it down on the table in front of us.

Unsuspecting diners would never know…

…that the reverse side held a big secret: the parfait glass indeed looked like it had been split straight down the middle!

▼ Even the grapes were cleanly sliced in half.

Thankfully, that didn’t mean the glass was in any danger of collapsing, but just that the vessel was only half the width of a regular one.

We had a train to catch soon, so it was time to dig in. It was still blowing our minds that even viewed from the top it looked like a perfectly ordinary parfait.

The Shine Muscat grapes were, as usual, tantalizingly sweet and refreshing. They meshed wonderfully with the layers of sorbet and jelly lining the inside of the glass. It felt good to know that we were still getting everything that we would from a normal parfait.

The sweet treat as a whole was truly the perfect size to feel full in a comfortable–not sickly–way.

Some readers might be asking, “Why not just order a mini parfait instead?” Mini parfaits in smaller glass dishes also exist at Denny’s Japan, so that’s always a possibility. However, we have to admit that there’s something special about the thrill of having a tall parfait placed in front of you that a shorter one just can’t replace.

Please note that not all Denny’s Japan locations may offer the Mapputatsu? Parfait. Those that do may not have all the same versions, either, so it’s best to check ahead of time if there’s a specific flavor that you want. We would strongly recommend the Shine Muscat variety–in fact, it was so good that we’re now hooked on anything with the same taste!
